reviews.reason: PrliAddonUpdates is never instantiated in the lite plugin — zero new PrliAddonUpdates() calls exist in the codebase — so the constructor and its hook registration are unreachable dead code within this plugin. Even if the Pro add-on instantiates the class at runtime, the registered hook fires only in the WP admin update screen and requires update_plugins capability; the sole callback check_incorrect_edition() at line 212 outputs a hardcoded, fully escaped admin URL string with no user-controlled input, presenting no attack surface.

counter_evidence.detail: Constructor is never called in the lite plugin. A codebase-wide search for 'new PrliAddonUpdates' returns zero results, confirming the class is defined but entirely unused within this plugin.

check_incorrect_edition() — the only callback registered on the dynamic hook — contains no user-controlled input. It calls PrliUtils::is_incorrect_edition_installed() and outputs a hardcoded admin_url() value wrapped in esc_url() and esc_html__(). No taint path exists.

The lite plugin already registers in_plugin_update_message-pretty-link/pretty-link.php with a concrete (non-dynamic) hook name directly in PrliUpdateController::load_hooks(). The PrliAddonUpdates class is a Pro-only add-on update helper that duplicates this pattern for arbitrary add-on slugs passed by the Pro plugin at runtime.
File is guarded by ABSPATH check at line 3, standard WordPress direct-access prevention.

missing_evidence: Pro add-on source (pretty-link-pro.php) to confirm what $main_file value is passed to the constructor and whether any non-trivial callback is registered on the resulting hook name.
Confirmation that PrliUtils::is_incorrect_edition_installed() does not produce any exploitable side effects (though the function name strongly implies a read-only boolean check).
dynamic_test_plan: Step 1: This finding does not warrant a dynamic test in the lite plugin — the class is never instantiated, so no hook is ever registered.
Step 2: If Pro add-on source becomes available, locate the new PrliAddonUpdates(...) call, extract the $main_file argument, and confirm the registered hook name.
Step 3: If hook is confirmed to fire, navigate to WP Admin > Plugins while logged in as admin and check if an update is shown for the Pro add-on.
Step 4: Observe the check_incorrect_edition() output — it should render only the hardcoded esc_url(admin_url(...)) link, with no reflected user input.
Step 5: Verify that the hook is inaccessible to any role below administrator (update_plugins capability required to reach the plugin update row).
